items.title: Hentoff Nat — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I once said to Jimmie Rowles, the master accompanist – I said, “What do you do when there’s no gigs?” “It’s all right,” he said. “I wait for the phone to ring.”

ctx.x: This question is almost unanswerable, but I’m going to ask it anyway: when Frankie Newton woke up in the morning, how do you think he assessed his life, his career, his lack of opportunity, his plight as a black man at that time? How did he – from how you knew him, how do you think he had a handle on . . .?

I would be presumptuous to answer that, but I will speculate, as we say, because he also had a very sharp ironic sense of humor. He probably woke up both angry and sardonic, and not giving up. That was the characteristic of all these guys I knew. That was part of being a musician – jazz musician. You didn’t give up. I once said to Jimmie Rowles, the master accompanist – I said, “What do you do when there’s no gigs?” “It’s all right,” he said. “I wait for the phone to ring.”
I’ve heard that, in a sense, Frankie Newton was blacklisted . . .
